title: Irrigated fresh tomatoes, watermelons and citrus are grown almost entirely for the home market (about 2.4-4.1% exported in 2022), and agricultural policy as assessed by the World Bank in 2014 was biased against exports, so export promotion is not the main driver of their water use

rootCauses.cause: State water mobilisation and on-farm incentives expanded irrigable land, and this expansion achieved national self-sufficiency in fruit and vegetables; output of fresh vegetables and citrus therefore goes mainly to the home market, with only small export volumes

Agricultural policy (as assessed by the World Bank in 2014 with 1990-2012 data) protected and subsidised continental products (cereals, milk, beef) and created an anti-export bias against Mediterranean crops
Growing domestic demand absorbs most citrus output; orchards are old and quality is average, which limits exports

In Cap Bon and central Tunisia, private irrigated perimeters grew citrus and vegetables by overdrawing groundwater; safeguard programmes then brought in transferred northern water, which drinking water now increasingly takes

dataGaps: Sidi Bouzid and Kairouan: no governorate-level series of irrigated vegetable area, crop mix or market destination was opened (CIHEAM and Cahiers Agricultures papers could not be downloaded). That their vegetables go to the domestic market is inferred from national export shares, not shown for these governorates.
Strawberry production and area: FAOSTAT shows a flat, estimated 10,000 t, which conflicts with the fast export-led growth reported in Cap Bon (SRC-TG-867). No official series was found.
Off-season (primeurs) and greenhouse vegetable exports: no product-level series separating early vegetables from seasonal production was opened.

Investment code advantages for export agriculture (1993 Code d'incitation aux investissements, fully exporting firms regime, 2016 investment law) and FOPRODEX support: only press coverage was found, no legal text opened, so their effect on crop choice is unknown.

EU-Tunisia agricultural protocol: the legal text was not opened. Sources disagree on tomatoes: a 18,816 t quota in 2010-2011 (SRC-TG-710) against unlimited duty-free access from 1 October to 31 May (SRC-TG-865).
Volumes of Medjerda-Cap Bon canal water going to citrus and vegetables against drinking water: only the qualitative statement that SONEDE withdrawals doubled since 1997 (SRC-TG-867).

Projection of the horticultural crop mix under water constraints: none found. Allocation projections exist (agricultural allocation 2,140 Mm3 in 2010 to 2,035 Mm3 in 2030, SRC-TG-864) but are a water-lane topic and do not break down by crop.
Figures on citrus, tomato and vegetable exports per crop from the FAO/CNEA report could not be used because its Table 29 rows are defective (SRC-TG-864).

excerpt: A common view holds that Tunisia drains its water by exporting thirsty fruit and vegetables such as tomatoes, watermelons, citrus and strawberries. The evidence does not support this for these crops. In 2022, official…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: A common view holds that Tunisia drains its water by exporting thirsty fruit and vegetables such as tomatoes, watermelons, citrus and strawberries. The evidence does not support this for these crops. In 2022, official FAOSTAT figures show exports of 27,264 t of fresh tomatoes out of 1.16 million t produced, 18,333 t of watermelons out of 450,000 t, and 12,638 t of oranges out of 345,000 t (SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863). These are export shares of about 2.4%, 4.1% and 3.7% (our calculation). Strawberry exports were 688 t (SRC-TG-863). Processed tomatoes are a partial exception: 33,416 t of tomato paste were exported in 2022, more than the fresh tomato tonnage that year even before converting paste to fresh equivalent, although paste exports were below fresh exports in 2020, 2021 and 2023 (SRC-TG-863), and tomato derivatives are named as an export product (SRC-TG-865). The fresh-equivalent share of tomato production exported as paste could not be computed. A French government brief states that fruit and vegetable production is mainly for domestic consumption, except citrus, dates and tomato and olive derived products (SRC-TG-865). The World Bank reports that domestic demand absorbs over 90% of citrus output (SRC-TG-710). The water used by irrigated fresh vegetables and citrus is therefore spent mainly on feeding the home market. Export-oriented water use is concentrated in dates and olive oil (FND-TG-860).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
The symptom is heavy irrigation of vegetables and citrus in water-short areas. The causes are domestic food policy and irrigation policy, not export promotion.

- **Past decision: irrigation expansion that achieved self-sufficiency.** Irrigable area rose from about 65,000 ha (1956) to over 496,000 ha (2015). The national studies centre states that this potential makes Tunisia self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables, with irrigated exports adding over 30% of agricultural exports (SRC-TG-864). Irrigated agriculture's share of agri-food exports was 24% in 1995, 33% in 2010 and 29% in 2014, and the same report calls this contribution "one of the major justifications" for irrigated agriculture (SRC-TG-864). Exports were thus part of the official case for irrigation. For fresh vegetables and citrus, however, the volumes exported remain small. The export value of irrigated agriculture is concentrated in dates (FND-TG-860); the per-crop breakdown in SRC-TG-864 is unusable.
- **Past decision: an anti-export bias.** Using 1990-2012 data (1990-2010 growth shares, 2000-2008 competitiveness, 1998-2011 quotas, 2008-2009 subsidies), the World Bank (2014) found that policy distorted production "away from Mediterranean products" toward cereals, milk and beef. Non-competitive products made up 39% of production but about 52% of sector growth, and protection introduced "an anti-export bias" (SRC-TG-710). In 2008-2009, irrigation subsidies were about 18% of input subsidies (SRC-TG-710). This contradicts the idea that export incentives pushed farmers into water-intensive horticulture. The same source rates Tunisia as competitive in tomatoes, oranges and potatoes (SRC-TG-710).
- **Symptom of the bias: unused export access.** Tunisia used about 55% of its EU citrus quota in 1998 and 60-62% in 2010-2011, 25% of its tomato quota in 1998 and 52-71% in 2010-2011, and about 20% of its conditioned olive oil quota (SRC-TG-710).
- **Regional pattern.** In Cap Bon, private perimeters developed citrus and vegetables "at the expense of" groundwater overexploitation. Safeguard programmes then brought in northern water (SRC-TG-864). From the late 1980s the state launched a water mobilisation programme to safeguard irrigated agriculture and supply urban drinking water, relying on five dams and the Medjerda-Cap Bon canal (SRC-TG-867). SONEDE's withdrawals from that canal have doubled since 1997, and the split has reversed in favour of drinking water (SRC-TG-867). In central Tunisia, the private irrigated sector is "dynamic" but overdraws shallow groundwater (SRC-TG-864).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- Production 2022 (official): tomatoes 1,160,000 t; watermelons 450,000 t; oranges 345,000 t (SRC-TG-862).
- Exports 2022: tomatoes 27,264 t; watermelons 18,333 t; oranges 12,638 t; strawberries 688 t; tomato paste 33,416 t of product. Exports 2023: tomatoes 25,434 t; watermelons 4,351 t; oranges 7,474 t; tomato paste 8,595 t (SRC-TG-863). Fresh tomato exports rose from 1,560 t in 2000 to 24,000-27,000 t in 2020-2023 (SRC-TG-863). They are growing fast, but from a low base.
- Orange exports were a larger share in the past: 22,214 t of 115,000 t in 2000 (about 19%) and 24,580 t of 136,700 t in 2010 (about 18%), against 3.7% in 2022 (our calculation, SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863). Recorded orange production nearly doubles between 2017 and 2018, which may be a series break, so part of the fall in the share may be statistical (SRC-TG-862).
- A peer-reviewed study agrees that tomatoes are "exported to a little extent" (SRC-TG-860). Vegetables' virtual water is about 60% blue (SRC-TG-861).
- Value per m3: irrigated vegetables returned 1.098 DT/m3 with the PNEEI programme and 1.234 DT/m3 without. Seasonal tomato and summer onion value water least among high-yield vegetables, while early pepper values it better (SRC-TG-864). Tomatoes have the highest blue economic water productivity of the main crops, at US$1.13/m3 for 1996-2005 (SRC-TG-868, relayed in SRC-TG-860).
- **Conflicting evidence on strawberries.** A 2013 IRMC field note says Cap Bon strawberry area is growing fast and is "mainly destined for export", extending peak irrigation demand from May to September (SRC-TG-867). FAOSTAT records only 688 t of exports in 2022, against an estimated production of about 10,000 t that has been flat for 20 years (SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863). The FAOSTAT production series is estimated or imputed, so the conflict cannot be settled here.
- **Conflicting evidence on EU tomato access.** One source gives an 18,816 t EU tomato quota for 2010-2011 (SRC-TG-710). Another gives unlimited duty-free access from 1 October to 31 May (SRC-TG-865).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content:
Medium. The national export shares rest on official FAOSTAT production and trade figures (tier A), but the shares are our own calculation and cover calendar years. The policy diagnosis rests on one World Bank chapter with 1990-2012 data (tier B). No current legal text on export incentives was opened, so the anti-export bias is documented only up to about 2012. The French government brief (tier B) supports only the destination of the produce, not the policy diagnosis, and it lists citrus as an export exception. Citrus is the weakest part of the domestic-market claim: oranges were about 18-19% exported in 2000-2010. The finding is weakest at regional level. No governorate data for Sidi Bouzid or Kairouan was opened, and the Cap Bon evidence is a 2013 research note plus a national typology. Off-season and greenhouse exports could not be separated, and these may be more export-oriented than the national totals suggest.

The finding refutes the framing only for fresh vegetables, watermelons, citrus and strawberries at national scale. It does not refute it for dates and olive oil (FND-TG-860).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water:** horticulture in Cap Bon and central Tunisia relies on overdrawn groundwater and, in Cap Bon, on water transferred through the Medjerda-Cap Bon canal. That transferred water is increasingly diverted to drinking water (SRC-TG-864, SRC-TG-867). The aquifer and transfer issues belong to the water lane.
- **Water allocation outlook:** the agricultural water allocation is planned to fall from 2,140 Mm3 (2010) to 2,035 Mm3 (2030), with per-hectare allocation down from about 4,700 to 4,050 m3 (SRC-TG-864). The crops that would absorb this cut are not specified.
- **Energy:** none found.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Programme national d'économie d'eau en irrigation (PNEEI) and its 2016 evaluation by SCET Tunisie (cited in SRC-TG-864).
- Programmes de sauvegarde des périmètres privés du Cap Bon using northern water transfers, and the Medjerda-Cap Bon canal managed by SECADENORD (SRC-TG-864, SRC-TG-867).
- Reorienting support from continental to Mediterranean products, and horizontal (non crop-specific) policies, as proposed by the World Bank (SRC-TG-710).
- Better use of EU preferential quotas for citrus and tomatoes, and harvest and post-harvest quality improvements for citrus (SRC-TG-710).
- Zoning crops by virtual water content and bioclimatic area (SRC-TG-861).

Chapter subtitle, p. 259 (printed):

> Tunisia does not have an agricultural policy; rather it has a food security policy, which goes against the potential of its agricultural sector

Box 9.1 discussion, pp. 261-262:

> not have a strong comparative advantage in cereals, which are intensive in land and are socially less profitable than arboriculture, fruits, and vegetables (box 9.1).

> Tunisia is also competitive in durum wheat (rain-fed and irrigated) and was also competitive in irrigated soft wheat when the international prices spiked in 2008, such that temporarily it became profitable to produce soft wheat in Tunisia. The competitiveness in soft wheat is limited to the irrigated areas and areas in the north and northwest regions where the rainfall is more favorable (not shown).

Section 9.2, p. 263:

> Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco.

> Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 265:

> pays inadequate quality bonuses for cereals, and caps the prices of processed foods.

p. 266:

> In 2009 the budgetary cost of food subsidies was approximately 1.5 percent of GDP, and this amount increased to over three percent of GDP in 2012 (table 9.3).

pp. 267-268:

> it is estimated that the annual cost of protecting employment in the cereals sector is four times the national per capita income.

> The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better--watered north and northwest parts of the country.

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

Additional extracts on Mediterranean and export crops (added for FND-TG-860/861). Page numbers follow the printed page footers, checked page by page:

Chapter introduction, p. 260:

> The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

p. 262:

> Tunisia is very competitive in production of olive oil and tomatoes (as shown by the DRC < 1) in each of the three years for which the analysis has been carried out (2000, 2004, and 2008). It is also competitive in production of oranges and potatoes, except in 2008 when the price of fertilizer was extremely high.

p. 262:

> The most competitive products, namely durum wheat, arboriculture (including fruit and olive oil), vegetables, and fisheries--which represent 58 percent of production over the last 20 years--contribute to the growth of the sector only up to about 46 percent, while non-competitive products (cereals, excluding durum wheat, beef, milk)--which concern 39 percent of production--contributed up to about 52 percent (table 9.1).

> in 1998 Tunisia used only approximately 55 percent of its citrus export quota (CNEA 2005b), and this amount was still only approximately 60 percent in 2010 and 2011

p. 263:

> Similarly, Tunisian used only 25 percent of its tomato quota in 1998 and still used only 50 to 70 percent of its quota in 2010 and 2011, respectively. Even for olive oil, Tunisia still manages to export only about 20 percent of its quota.

> For other products, such as tomatoes, the shortfalls in taking advantage of these export opportunities is also due to the fact that the EU import quotas are subject to specific calendars which further restrict their use.

Box 9.2, p. 264:

> Citrus production has stagnated for more than a decade, and growing domestic demand absorbs more than 90 percent of local production. Current citrus exports to the EU amount to 24,000 tons and represent only 60 percent of the country's preferential quota.

Table 9.2, p. 265, "Exports to the EU for Selected Products under Quota, 2010 and 2011" (tons 2010 | 2011 | EU quota | % of quota 2010 | 2011; source Tunisia Ministry of Agriculture):

> Citrus fruit 24580 23610 39355 62 60

> Tomatoes 9820 13384 18816 52 71

> Olive oil (conditioned) 10877 12035 56000 19 21

pp. 265-266:

> The focus of farmers on products in which Tunisia is not competitive is the direct result of existing agricultural policies. In fact much of the growth in agriculture has been driven by subsidies and the trade protection of products in which Tunisia is not competitive.

> In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent).

pp. 268-269:

> The bias introduced by protection of selected agricultural products results in a reallocation of capital and labor toward those overprotected products at the expense of alternative products in which Tunisia's exports have a comparative advantage, thus introducing an anti-export bias.

Additional extracts on the support framework, budget transfers and simulations (added for FND-TG-920/921/922). Page numbers here follow the printed page footers of the PDF (the footer number closes each page), which may differ by one or two from the page references above:

Chapter opening (p. 260):

> This chapter suggests that Tunisia does not really have an agricultural policy but has instead a food security policy that in fact hinders the development of its agricultural sector. The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

Section 9.2, p. 265:

> Agricultural production increased by 67 percent (in value) over the period 1990-2010, but almost one-third (17 percent of the value) originates in bovine beef and milk, in which Tunisia is not competitive.

p. 265:

> Market price support is significant, accounting for over 30 percent of total budgetary transfers to agriculture in recent years [...] Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco. [...] Market price support is particularly important in the milk sector, which accounts for over 50 percent of expenditure on market price support in recent years. Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 266:

> The simple average of the "most favored nation" (MFN) rates applied to agri-food products is 24.6 percent (compared to 16.5 percent for all products), with a maximum rate of 36 percent. > Input subsidies (such as improved seeds, forage seeds, energy, irrigation water, and so on) also play an important role and account for approximately 20 to 25 percent of total budgetary transfers in recent years: In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent). Fertilizer subsidies were discontinued in 1991.

> The budgetary direct costs of policies reached approximately 0.8 percent of GDP in 2010 (or TND 350 million) [...] although Tunisia committed (in the framework of the 1994 Uruguay Round of trade negotiations) to reduce the overall mass of domestic support (from 76 million to 66 million dollars), in fact the budget expenditure for agricultural support has been steadily increasing [...] Between 2000 and 2009 the share of market price support and input subsidies increased from 31 to 53 percent while those of investment aid [...] and those intended for general services actually decreased

p. 267:

> the World Bank estimates that the net effect of trade protection of agricultural goods is equivalent to a loss of approximately four percent of consumer spending if the consumer purchases remain constant, and approximately 5.6 percent if consumers readjust their spending in response to changes in relative prices (table 9.4) (for a full discussion of the model and these results see World Bank 2006)

> the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural products would increase GDP by approximately 0.8 percent [...] However, the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural goods would also cause a loss of approximately 87,000 jobs from agriculture that would have to be absorbed by other sectors.

Table 9.4 (p. 268), "Effects on the Entire Economy of Opening Up Trade in Agricultural Goods", source CGE model simulations, World Bank (2006). Rows (baseline / full liberalisation with EU agricultural subsidies / without EU agricultural subsidies):

> Economic growth (% per year, in the years following liberalization) 5.7 / 6.5 / 6.2
> Labor force transferred to other sectors (in thousand jobs) - / 87 / 67
> Gains of adjustment (million TND through 2025) - / 7107 / 4441

p. 268:

> Using a linear programming model [...] the World Bank estimates that nearly 70 percent of farms would gain from the removal of price distortions in the agricultural sector (table 9.5). [...] The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better-watered north and northwest parts of the country.

p. 269:

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

> Agricultural producers who operate in filieres (sectors) that hold great promise (for example, dried fruit, olive oil, fruit, and vegetables), prevalently in interior regions, often receive little or no support from agricultural policies and have great difficulty in accessing financing, inputs, information, or advice

Box 9.3 (p. 270), farmer testimony:

> despite the recognized quality of its olive oil, Tunisia is still using only 20 percent of its quota of exports to the European Union.

Recommendations section (pp. 273-274):

> (a) Progressively shift away from price support and orient agricultural policy toward direct income support

> Taking action to improve access to finance for the agricultural sector. Access to finance is especially challenging for investments in arboriculture (olive oil and fruit), which entail several years between the initial investment and the start of the production phase.
resolvedSources.notes: Chapter of the World Bank Development Policy Review published in 2014; underlying analyses date from 2006-2012 (CGE model World Bank 2006; DRC analysis World Bank 2009 using 2000, 2004, 2008 prices). Its view that cereal producers receive market price support contrasts with the 2024 World Bank statement that farmgate prices were below import parity (SRC-TG-705); the two describe different periods and price contexts. The DRC table extracted with shifted values and is not quoted; only prose is used.

resolvedSources.title: Virtual water trade patterns in relation to environmental and socioeconomic factors: A case study for Tunisia
resolvedSources.publisher: Science of the Total Environment 613-614 (2018) 287-297; authors Chouchane H., Krol M.S., Hoekstra A.Y.; doi 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.09.032
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract (p. 287):

> "The results show that NVWI during the study period for the selected crops is not influenced by blue water scarcity. NVWI correlates in two alternative models to either population and precipitation (model I) or to GDP and irrigated area (model II). The models are better in explaining NVWI of staple crops (wheat, barley, potatoes) than NVWI of cash crops (dates, olives, tomatoes)."

Section 2 (p. 288), crop selection:

> "for Tunisian export (olives and dates, which together account for 45% of the total agricultural export value in 2010; FAOSTAT, 2015), and the two crops with highest economic blue water productivity in the country (tomatoes and potatoes; see Chouchane et al., 2015). Wheat and barley are mainly rain-fed and net imported. Olives are rain-fed and dates are mainly irrigated. Both tomatoes and potatoes are mainly irrigated, while tomatoes are exported to a little extent and potatoes are mainly imported (Ministry of Agriculture, 2011)."

Table 1 (p. 288), average 1981-2010 (columns: production 10^3 t/yr; % irrigated production; net import 10^3 t/yr; economic blue water productivity US$/m3):

> "Olives 720 | 39 | -100 | 0.03"
> "Dates 95 | 100 | -30 | 0.11"
> "Tomatoes 690 | 100 | -2.2 | 1.13"
> "Potatoes 250 | 98 | 30 | 0.97"
> "Wheat 1100 | 22 | 1100 | 0.12"

Section 2.2 (p. 290):

> "The export of olive oil, dates, wheat and tomatoes accounts for 72% of the total crop-related virtual water export (68% for olive oil only) over the period 1996-2005 (Chouchane et al., 2015)."

Table 5 (p. 291), average WF per unit of crop, m3/tonne, 1981-2010 (green | blue | total):

> "Olives 7100 | 420 | 7500"
> "Dates 650 | 5000 | 5600"
> "Tomatoes 140 | 180 | 320"
> "Wheat 4100 | 550 | 4700"

Section 3 (p. 291-292):

> "net virtual water exports related to cash crops (olive oil, dates and tomatoes) are increasing as well."

> "In model II, an increase in irrigated land by 1000 ha increases the net virtual water export of dates by 5.6 Mm3."

Discussion (p. 295):

> "Dates and olives, the most exported crops in Tunisia, have the highest total WF per unit among the selected crops. Dates have the highest blue water footprint in m3/tonne. Additionally, dates are only produced in the south of Tunisia, the region with the highest scarcity level (Chouchane et al., 2015). A remaining question is why a water-scarce country continues producing a blue water intensive crop like dates for export. The selected variables of this study couldn't answer this question; other factors must be the reason. Dates have also a low economic water productivity and from an economic perspective reallocating the water used by dates for growing other crops, with higher water productivity, such as potatoes and tomatoes would be more beneficial (Chouchane et al., 2015)."

> "there are other factors that could influence the virtual water trade in a country that are not included in current study, such as: agricultural policies, value of water, international prices, etc."
resolvedSources.notes: AquaCrop-based water footprints, six crops, 1981-2010. Excludes grey water. Water availability from Ministry of Agriculture data without environmental flows. Data period ends 2010; date area and exports have grown strongly since (see SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863). Economic blue water productivity values come from Chouchane et al. (2015), not recomputed here; they match the 1996-2005 "blue EWP in irrigated agriculture" column of Chouchane et al. (2013) Table 8 (SRC-TG-868), so they are 1996-2005 values even though Table 1 is headed 1981-2010.

resolvedSources.title: Quantification of Virtual Water balance of Tunisia: Flows Embedded in the main produced, consumed and exchanged Agricultural Commodities
resolvedSources.publisher: New Medit (CIHEAM) n. 2/2017, pp. 11-18; authors Makhlouf M., Frija A., Chebil A., Souissi A., Stambouli T., Benalaya A.
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract (p. 11):

> "Our calculations show that Tunisia is a net virtual water "importer". We also surprisingly show that, even though olive production is mostly rain fed, olive oil production is still identified as the most water-demanding commodity (7 m3/kg) in Tunisia due to the need of blue water for its processing. By exporting 145.9 thousand tons of olive oil and 97.8 thousand tons of date in 2013, Tunisia has respectively lost 1079.6 and 283.6 Million m3 of virtual water. On the other hand, by importing 2146.6 thousand tons of cereals and 15.7 thousand tons of potato in the same year, Tunisia has respectively saved 2901.7 and 3.14 Million m3 of water resources."

Résumé (p. 11, French version of the abstract):

> "Nos calculs montrent que la Tunisie est un pays "importateur net " d'eau virtuelle."

English gloss: Our calculations show that Tunisia is a net importer of virtual water.

Section 4 (results, p. 14-15):

> "Unlike grain, the blue virtual water content of vegetable represents around 60% of the total virtual water content due to a couple of reasons such as the period of cultivation which is summer wherein the crop water requirement is the highest"

> "The results obtained show that, more than 80% of the virtual water exported is blue virtual water."

Section 5 (discussion, p. 16-17):

> "Results show that commodities such as olives, almond, oats and barley are among the crops with higher share of green water content compared to the share of blue water (Chouchane et al., 2013). Most of these crops are not traded (exported) and are consumed locally. Concerning virtual water trade, our results show that Tunisia is essentially exporting blue water. This is especially due to the high contribution of water intensive crops such as dates and olive oil to the agricultural export of Tunisia."

Conclusion (p. 17):

> "Finally, it was also shown that Tunisia is a net importer of virtual water. But we believe this is not intentional and is simply due to its dependency from international markets for the import of many necessary food commodities such as cereals, animal feeds, and vegetable oils."
resolvedSources.notes: Based on the authors' field surveys across bioclimatic zones (single year 2013 for trade flows). The numeric values of Table 1 (virtual water content by crop, including irrigated maltaise citrus and irrigated tomato) and Table 2 could not be extracted: the PDF uses an embedded font whose glyphs do not map to text. The claim that olive oil is 7 m3/kg "due to the need of blue water for its processing" conflicts with SRC-TG-860, which puts olives at 7,100 m3/t green and 420 m3/t blue; the two studies use different methods and system boundaries. Implied blue+green content of exported dates in 2013 is about 2,900 m3/t (283.6 Mm3 / 97.8 kt), lower than the 5,600 m3/t total (5,000 blue) in SRC-TG-860. FAOSTAT records 2013 date exports as 105,803 t (SRC-TG-863), not the 97.8 kt used in the paper, so the implied per-tonne value is approximate.

resolvedSources.notes: Production figures for 2022 are flagged official (A) and are the latest official year for most crops; 2023 values are imputed. Several area series are unreliable and should not be used: olives 2020 (3.6 Mha, estimated, larger than Tunisia's olive area), oranges 2020 (5,214 ha imputed, half the adjacent years), watermelon area (falls 80% from 2000 to 2023 while output rises 59%). Strawberry production is flat at about 10,000 t for two decades and estimated/imputed after 2020, which conflicts with the rapid growth of strawberry area reported for Cap Bon (SRC-TG-867); treat it as unknown. Date area flags are official (A) for 2000, 2009, 2011 and 2013-2016, imputed for 2010 and 2012, and imputed or estimated from 2017 onwards; the 2022 imputed value (77,404 ha) is about 35% above the ministry figure of 57,385 ha relayed by ONAGRI (SRC-TG-743). Orange production nearly doubles between 2017 (186,900 t) and 2018 (346,000 t), both official; this may be a series break, so long-run comparisons of orange export shares should be read with care.

resolvedSources.title: Évaluation de l'approvisionnement alimentaire dans un contexte de pénurie d'eau dans la région NENA. Application de l'approche courbe de coût d'approvisionnement alimentaire. Cas de la Tunisie
resolvedSources.publisher: FAO, prepared by Centre National des Études Agricoles (CNEA), Rome; ISBN 978-92-5-130826-4
resolvedSources.extracts:
Summary (p. xx):

> "En tant que pays manquant fondamentalement de ressources hydriques, la Tunisie a intérêt à importer le maximum possible de produits agricoles consommateurs d'eau afin de compenser ses déficits internes alimentaires et hydriques, tout en exportant des produits agricoles à faible consommation d'eau et de haute valeur ajoutée."

English gloss: As a country fundamentally short of water, Tunisia has an interest in importing as many water-consuming agricultural products as possible to offset its internal food and water deficits, while exporting agricultural products with low water use and high added value.

Summary (p. xviii):

> "La demande moyenne actuelle en eau par hectare réellement irrigué est estimée à 4 500 m³. Il est à remarquer, cependant, que cette demande est assez variable selon les cultures et les zones climatiques: elle peut se réduire à 1 000 et 2000 m³/ha pour les céréales et fourrages au nord et atteindre 15 000 à 20 000 m³/ha pour les palmiers dattiers dans les oasis du sud."

English gloss: Average water demand per actually irrigated hectare is about 4,500 m3; it ranges from 1,000-2,000 m3/ha for cereals and fodder in the north to 15,000-20,000 m3/ha for date palms in the southern oases.

Introduction (p. 1):

> "Entre 1956 et 2015, le taux de mobilisation des ressources hydrauliques est passé de 8 à 90 pour cent, le nombre des grands barrages s'est accru de 3 à 34, les puits de surface ont vu leur nombre multiplié par 46 et les sondages par 11 et les superficies irrigables estimées à environ 65 000 ha en 1956 (irrigués presque totalement à partir de puits de surface et de sources naturelles) dépassent 496 000 ha en 2015. Ce potentiel de production agricole indéniable permet à la Tunisie d'être autosuffisante en fruits et légumes et contribue largement à l'équilibre de la balance alimentaire du pays par les exportations qui représentent plus de 30 pour cent des exportations agricoles totales."

English gloss: Between 1956 and 2015 water mobilisation rose from 8 to 90%, large dams from 3 to 34, surface wells x46, boreholes x11, and irrigable area from about 65,000 ha (1956) to over 496,000 ha (2015). This makes Tunisia self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables, and irrigated exports are over 30% of total agricultural exports.

> "L'accroissement soutenu des superficies irrigables bénéficiant de grands investissements dans la mobilisation de l'eau, les nombreuses incitations financières très généreuses pour l'équipement à la parcelle et la politique de soutien des prix de l'eau d'irrigation a largement contribué à la sécurité alimentaire du pays."

English gloss: Sustained growth of irrigable area, backed by large investment in water mobilisation, very generous financial incentives for on-farm equipment and support to irrigation water prices, contributed greatly to the country's food security.

Section 2.8.7 (p. 67), irrigated agriculture in exports:

> "Les exportations: l'examen des données portant sur les exportations agricoles montre que la part de l'agriculture irriguée dans cet agrégat est relativement importante. Cette part est estimée, comme le montre le tableau suivant à 24 pour cent des exportations agricoles et agroalimentaires en 1995. Cette part a augmenté pour se situer à 33 pour cent de ce même agrégat en 2010 et à 29 pour cent en 2014. Cette contribution constitue en réalité l'une des justifications majeures de l'agriculture irriguée."

English gloss: Irrigated agriculture's share of agricultural and agri-food exports was 24% in 1995, 33% in 2010 and 29% in 2014; this contribution is one of the main justifications for irrigated agriculture.

Table 29 (p. 67), totals only, 1000 DT. Total agricultural and agri-food exports: 1995 462 000; 2000 628 000; 2005 1 225 600; 2010 1 647 800; 2014 2 048 800. Total irrigated agriculture exports: 108 700; 133 700; 265 900; 541 500; 589 600. Share (%): 24; 21; 22; 33; 29. Source line: "MARHP, annuaire statistique agricole 2012 et budget économique 2015".

Section 2.8 (p. 73), Table 33, water valorisation with and without the national irrigation water-saving programme (PNEEI), source SCET Tunisie 2016. Columns: water valorisation (DT/m³), water charges / total charges, water productivity (kg/m³):

> "Maraîchage — Avec PNEEI 1,098 14,1% 5,251; Sans PNEEI 1,234 13,4% 3,483"

> "Les résultats sont plus contrastés en maraîchage. Parmi les cultures qui ont les plus forts rendements, la tomate de saison et l'oignon d'été sont également celles qui valorisent le moins bien l'eau, au contraire du piment primeur."

English gloss: Results for vegetables are mixed. Among the highest-yielding crops, seasonal tomato and summer onion give the lowest value per m3, unlike early-season pepper.

Section on allocations (p. 54):

> "Ainsi, l'allocation moyenne à l'hectare passerait d'environ 4 700 m³/ha dans les années 2010 à 4 050 m³/ha à l'horizon 2030. L'allocation totale au secteur serait ainsi revue de 2 140 Mm³/an en 2010 à 2 035 Mm³/an en 2030."

English gloss: The average allocation per hectare would fall from about 4,700 m3/ha in the 2010s to 4,050 m3/ha by 2030; total allocation to the sector would go from 2,140 Mm3/yr in 2010 to 2,035 Mm3/yr in 2030.

Typology of irrigated perimeter groups (p. 139-140):

> "3. Le groupe des périmètres de types «Cap Bon»: il est caractérisé par des périmètres privés assez importants et des systèmes agrumicoles et maraîchers relativement développés mais aux dépens d'une surexploitation des ressources en eaux souterraines. Des programmes de sauvegarde des périmètres privés ont été engagés grâce aux transferts des eaux du Nord."

English gloss: Cap Bon-type perimeters have large private perimeters with well-developed citrus and vegetable systems, but at the cost of groundwater overexploitation. Safeguard programmes for private perimeters were launched using transfers of northern water.

> "4. Le groupe des périmètres de la Tunisie Centrale: il se distingue par un secteur irrigué privé assez dynamique mais au prix de la surexploitation des ressources phréatiques."

English gloss: Central Tunisia perimeters have a dynamic private irrigated sector, at the price of overexploiting shallow groundwater.

> "6. Le groupe des périmètres du Sud (Oasis maritimes, Oasis continentales, périmètres du Sud-est): Il se caractérise par l'exploitation intensive des eaux quasi fossiles dans les oasis et l'extension parfois illicite de celles-ci dans certaines zones (Kébili). La valorisation de l'eau sur le plan économique y est encore faible en raison de la tendance vers la monoculture du palmier dattier (filière dattes développée) et une consommation d'eau des plus élevées (15 000 à 20 000 m3/ha)."

English gloss: Southern perimeters rely on intensive use of near-fossil water and sometimes illegal oasis extensions (Kebili). Economic water value is still low because of the trend toward date palm monoculture and very high water use (15,000-20,000 m3/ha).
resolvedSources.notes: Report by the national agricultural studies centre (CNEA) for FAO. In Table 29 the per-crop rows (dates, citrus, fruit and vegetable derivatives, vegetables) are defective in the PDF: their values repeat those of Table 28 (milk, potatoes, sugar) and do not sum to the stated totals, so only the totals and the share line are used. Page numbers are printed page numbers (roman for the summary). The 2030 allocation figures come from DGEDA/MARH "Eau 21" updates cited in the report.

resolvedSources.title: Les politiques agricoles à travers le monde : quelques exemples. Tunisie (fiche pays 2014)
resolvedSources.publisher: Ministère de l'Agriculture, de l'Agroalimentaire et de la Forêt (France)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Section 1, production (p. 2):

> "La production de fruits et légumes est essentiellement destinée à la consommation interne, à l'exception des agrumes, des dattes et des produits dérivés de la tomate et de l'olive."

English gloss: Fruit and vegetable production is mainly for domestic consumption, except citrus, dates, and tomato and olive derived products.

> "La production d'agrumes couvre 17 200 ha et permet des exportations, en particulier les oranges, destinées essentiellement à la France."

English gloss: Citrus covers 17,200 ha and allows exports, especially oranges, mostly to France.

Section on EU relations (p. 5):

> "à ce jour, l'UE a toutefois accordé à la Tunisie des préférences tarifaires à un certain nombre de produits. Par exemple, la Tunisie dispose aujourd'hui d'un accès illimité à droit nul du 1er octobre au 31 mai pour ses tomates. Un contingent tarifaire lui a également été accordé sur l'huile d'olive (56 700 t)."

English gloss: The EU has granted Tunisia tariff preferences on some products: unlimited duty-free access from 1 October to 31 May for tomatoes, and a tariff quota of 56,700 t for olive oil.
resolvedSources.notes: French government country brief, short and secondary. Its statement of unlimited duty-free tomato access from October to May differs from the 18,816 t EU tomato quota in a Tunisian Ministry of Agriculture table reproduced by the World Bank for 2010-2011 (SRC-TG-710); the two may describe different regimes (seasonal unlimited window versus a quota outside it) or different years. The legal text of the EU-Tunisia agricultural protocol was not opened.

resolvedSources.title: Concurrences et conflits pour l'usage de l'eau en Tunisie : Etude de cas dans la région du Cap Bon
resolvedSources.publisher: IRMC (Institut de recherche sur le Maghreb contemporain), Bulletin trimestriel n° 12, septembre-décembre 2013; authors Alia Gana (CNRS) with Benjamin Fouillen
resolvedSources.extracts:
p. 21:

> "Le Cap-Bon est traditionnellement une région de culture maraîchère et fruitière intensive, qui fournit environ 16 % de la production agricole nationale, avec seulement 4 % de la SAU totale du pays. Il s'agit principalement de la production d'agrumes, de tomates, de pommes de terre et de la viticulture. Le développement de l'agriculture intensive et de cultures fortement consommatrices en eau y ont entrainé une surexploitation et une dégradation des eaux souterraines qui se traduit par une chute de la piézométrie et une baisse de la qualité des eaux, notamment en raison de l'intrusion marine."

English gloss: Cap Bon is traditionally a region of intensive vegetable and fruit growing, providing about 16% of national agricultural output on 4% of the country's farmland, mainly citrus, tomatoes, potatoes and vines. Intensive agriculture and very water-consuming crops caused overexploitation and degradation of groundwater, with falling water tables and lower quality, notably through seawater intrusion.

> "Ceci a conduit les pouvoirs publics à mettre en oeuvre, dès la fin des années 1980, un vaste programme de mobilisation des ressources en eau pour la sauvegarde de l'agriculture irriguée et l'approvisionnement en eau potable des zones urbaines. Les infrastructures existantes incluent cinq barrages, auxquels s'ajoute le canal Medjerda-Cap Bon qui assure le transfert des eaux du Nord"

English gloss: This led the authorities, from the late 1980s, to launch a large water mobilisation programme to safeguard irrigated agriculture and supply urban drinking water. Infrastructure includes five dams plus the Medjerda-Cap Bon canal, which transfers northern water.

p. 22:

> "Les prélèvements effectués par la SONEDE sur le canal Medjerda Cap Bon ont doublé depuis 1997 et aujourd'hui la répartition des volumes prélevés entre usages agricoles et non agricoles s'est inversée en faveur de la consommation en eau potable."

English gloss: SONEDE's withdrawals from the Medjerda-Cap Bon canal have doubled since 1997, and the split between agricultural and non-agricultural uses has reversed in favour of drinking water.

> "Enfin, l'augmentation des besoins pour l'irrigation est liée au développement de cultures spéculatives plus consommatrices en eau, en particulier le développement de la culture de la fraise, dont les superficies s'accroissent à un rythme rapide et qui sont principalement destinées à l'exportation. Cette évolution a non seulement pour conséquence d'augmenter les besoins quantitatifs en eau, mais également d'étendre la période de pointe de la demande en eau, qui s'étale désormais de mai à septembre."

English gloss: Finally, rising irrigation needs are linked to the development of more water-consuming speculative crops, in particular strawberries, whose area is growing fast and which are mainly for export. This raises water needs and extends the peak demand period, now from May to September.
resolvedSources.notes: Preliminary research note (programme Sicmed/Mistrals-IRD/INRGREF/CNRS) based on interviews in the Lebna catchment, not a peer-reviewed article. It gives no figures for strawberry area or export volumes. The claim that strawberries are "mainly for export" is not matched by FAOSTAT, which reports about 690 t exported in 2022 against an estimated 10,000 t production (SRC-TG-862, SRC-TG-863); FAOSTAT strawberry production is itself estimated, so the conflict is unresolved.

resolvedSources.title: Water footprint of Tunisia from an economic perspective (Value of Water Research Report Series No. 61)
resolvedSources.publisher: UNESCO-IHE Institute for Water Education, Delft; authors Chouchane H., Hoekstra A.Y., Krol M.S., Mekonnen M.M.
resolvedSources.extracts:
Summary (p. 5):

> "At national level, tomatoes and potatoes were the main crops with relatively high economic water productivity, with a Tunisian average of 1.08 and 0.87 US$/m3 respectively, while olives and barley were the main crops with relatively low productivity, of 0.03 and 0.04 US$/m3 respectively. In terms of economic land productivity, oranges had the highest productivity, with 4040 US$/ha, and barley the lowest, with 130 US$/ha."

Section 3 (p. 13):

> "Dates, almonds, figs and grapes are the biggest blue water users with 3270, 1950, 1740 and 1080 m3/ton respectively."

> "The total blue WF is dominated by dates and olives (together 47%) and, to a lesser extent grapes, wheat and almonds."

Table 4 (p. 14), "The average green, blue and grey water footprint of main crops in Tunisia (1996-2005)". Columns: total WF (Mm3/yr) green | blue | grey | total; WF per ton (m3/ton) green | blue | grey | total; source Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011a):

> "Dates 110 350 10 470 | 1030 3270 80 4390"
> "Olives 7270 270 30 7570 | 8790 330 40 9150"
> "Tomatoes 50 40 10 100 | 60 50 10 120"

Table 8 (p. 19), "Physical and economic water productivity of main crops in Tunisia at national level (1996-2005)". Economic water productivity columns (US$/m3): total (green) EWP in rain-fed | green EWP in irrigated | blue EWP in irrigated | total EWP in irrigated | average EWP in irrigated and rain-fed; producer price US$/kg precedes them:

> "Dates ... 1.01 | 0.40 0.62 0.11 0.23 0.23"
> "Tomatoes ... 0.12 | 1.26 1.03 1.13 1.07 1.08"
> "Potatoes ... 0.21 | 0.80 0.77 0.97 0.88 0.87"

p. 19:

> "In terms of total ELP, oranges, tomatoes and dates had the highest ELPs, with 4040, 3770 and 3080 US$/ha respectively, while barley and olives had the lowest ELPs, with 130 and 170 US$/ha respectively."

p. 20:

> "Dates and oranges had relatively low economic water productivities (0.23 and 0.58 US$/ m3 respectively) as compared to potatoes (0.87 US$/ m3) (see Table 8), but the ELPs for dates and oranges were higher (3080 and 4040 US$/ha respectively) than the ELP for potatoes (2870 US$/ha)."

> "At a national level, the figures on economic water productivities (Table 8) provide little basis for understanding or explaining current cropping patterns. The figures on economic land productivities give a better basis for understanding, because various of the crops with large production volumes (especially tomatoes, potatoes, oranges and dates) have a relatively high ELP."
resolvedSources.notes: Research report from the same group as SRC-TG-860 (Chouchane et al. 2018), so it is only partly independent. It uses the Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011) global model for 1996-2005, whereas SRC-TG-860 uses AquaCrop for 1981-2010. It gives a lower blue water footprint for dates (3,270 m3/t against 5,000 in SRC-TG-860). The economic blue water productivities quoted in SRC-TG-860 Table 1 (dates 0.11, tomatoes 1.13, potatoes 0.97 US$/m3) are the "blue EWP in irrigated agriculture" values of Table 8 here, for 1996-2005, not 1981-2010 averages. Not peer-reviewed (report series), so tier B.

relatedItems.title: Dates are the export crop that ships Tunisia's scarce blue water abroad: exports grew about sixfold from 2000 to 2022 on the crop with the highest blue water footprint per tonne among Tunisia's main crops and a low return per m3
Tunisia imports roughly half of its cereals and almost all of its soft (bread) wheat, even in good harvest years
The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
